study.title: Deuteronomy 11: love, memory and choice before the promised land
study.overview: Moses concludes his exhortation by calling Israel to love the LORD with concrete obedience, remembering the works already seen from God in Egypt, in the sea, in the wilderness and in the judgment of rebels. The chapter contrasts the promised land with Egypt, presents the dependence on the rain and divine blessing, and places before the people two ways: fidelity that leads to life, to the possession of the land and to prosperity, or infidelity that brings curse, scarcity and expulsion. The climax is a serious call: to keep and to practice all the statutes and judgments of the LORD.

outline.title: Love to God based on the memory of the works of the Lord
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the commandment to love the Lord and continually obey. Moses appeals to what the people saw: the punishment in Egypt, the power of God in the sea, in the wilderness, and in the judgment on Dathan and Abiram. Obedience is not abstract; it is born of the reverent remembrance of what God has already done before their eyes.

outline.title: Obedience that strengthens, sustains and makes fruitful
outline.explanation: The keeping of the commandments is linked to the entrance and permanence on the earth. The promised land is described as dependent on the rain of the sky and the constant care of the LORD, unlike Egypt, which required continuous human effort of irrigation. The promise includes agricultural sustenance and abundance, showing that life on earth depends on God's faithfulness and the obedient response of the people.

outline.title: The danger of idolatry and the promise of victory
outline.explanation: Moses warns against the deceit of the heart, idolatry, and the separation of the LORD. The disobedience closes the heavens and produces loss of the earth; fidelity, on the contrary, records the Word in the heart, in the house and in the education of the children, and leads to the expulsion of the opposing nations, the expansion of the territory and the fear that God will place on enemies.

outline.title: Blessing and curse before Israel
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with a public and solemn decision: blessing for those who hear and curse to those who reject. Gerizim and Ebal serve as a landmark of this choice. Israel is about to cross the Jordan, and therefore needs to keep and practice all the statutes and rights presented by Moses.

study.context: Moses speaks to Israel at the gates of entry into the promised land, resuming the commandments and judgments that must be obeyed in the national and religious life of the people. The chapter presupposes the recent experience of the exodus, the desert and the imminent crossing of the Jordan. The mentions of Gerizim, Ebal, Gilgal and the campinas de Moré function as references related to the possession of the land and the solemnity of the covenant commitment.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that love for God is not mere inner affection, but obedient loyalty. Obedience appears as an answer to the already experienced grace: God has delivered, sustained and judged for his people. The promised land is a gift, but also a place of responsibility; in it, the life of Israel depends on the sovereign care of the LORD, symbolized by rain and fertility. The text also shows the seriousness of idolatry: to depart from God brings disorder, dryness and loss. At the same time, the Word must dwell in the heart and be transmitted to children, because fidelity to the covenant involves memory, worship, family and public life. Blessing and curse are not random, but correspond to the people's response to God's commandments.

scholarViews.insight: In covenant language, blessing is the result of obedience, while the curse stems from disobedience; the verse prepares the section of chapters 27-28.
Moses connects the commandment to love the LORD to the memory of what God has already done, showing that obedience is born of gratitude and awareness of divine works.
The promised land is presented as dependent on the rain of the sky and the direct care of God, unlike Egypt, where irrigation required constant human effort.

questions: How does the remembrance of God's past works strengthen obedience today?
What concrete signs show when the heart is turning to modern idols?
How can instruction of the Word within the home be more intentional and everyday?
study.practice: The chapter calls the reader to turn memory into obedience. A concrete practice is to review, in family or alone, the actions of God already perceived in life and, from this, choose a specific discipline of fidelity: daily prayer, biblical teaching to children, rejection of commitments that compete with God and practical trust in the care of the LORD rather than anxiety. It is also worth examining where security is sought: in human resources or in the God that gives rain, sustenance and direction.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not accurately define Gilgal's exact location or some geographical landmarks; therefore, this part was treated with caution. It is also not possible to confirm from the notes the exact meaning of all old terms beyond the explanations already given by the commentators. Confessional interpretations were presented as theological reading, not as indisputable conclusions of the text.
